---
title: "Ranking models for UK All-Weather Flat handicaps: the exploded conditional logit and the place market"
subtitle: "Paper 2b in a series on UK All-Weather racing outcomes"
author: "Patrick Gillen"
date: today
abstract: |
  Paper 2a established a win-prediction model on UK All-Weather Flat
  handicaps using an extended feature set and race-level interactions.
  This paper asks a different question: can the same feature set, fitted
  under a ranking objective rather than a win objective, predict the top-3
  finishing order better than the betting market? We fit the exploded
  conditional logit — equivalent to maximising the Plackett–Luce
  likelihood over the top-3 — using the feature set defined in paper 2a.
  We evaluate against a market baseline derived from win starting prices
  via discounted Harville (Lo & Bacon-Shone). [Results to be completed.]

  html: default

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

This is the second of the two papers that split the original paper 2. Its
companion, paper 2a, fixed the prediction objective as the *win* and asked
how far an enriched feature set could narrow the gap to the betting
market; the answer was a modest improvement, with the market still
leading. This paper holds that feature set fixed and changes the
*objective*: instead of predicting which horse wins, we predict the top-3
finishing *order*, fitting the exploded conditional logit — the
Plackett–Luce ranking model — on the same features. The question is
whether a ranking objective recovers more of the market's edge than the
win objective did. @sec-data points to paper 2a for the shared data and
feature set and constructs the place-market baseline against which the
model is judged; @sec-exploded-model fits the ranking model;
@sec-evaluation evaluates it on ranking metrics; and @sec-discussion draws
the conclusions.

# Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

I have been interested in modelling horse racing since first
acquiring the Smartform database more than a decade ago. The project
has been picked up and put down many times, the obstacle almost
always being the gap between an idea and a running implementation.
What is different now is that working alongside Claude Code
(Anthropic's coding agent), with web-based Claude as a research
companion, has compressed that gap dramatically. I am grateful to
my brother, Michael Gillen, for the suggestion to build the model
on All-Weather races — the foundation of the scope choices set out
in @sec-data. The design choices — dataset, scope, model,
comparison, editorial line — are mine. The implementation, the bulk
of the draft prose, and a great deal of the verification were
Claude Code's, under my direction; every output was reviewed and
edited before it reached the paper. I do not yet know what general
lessons this experiment points to about the value of human–AI
collaboration in applied statistics. That uncertainty is part of
why I am doing the work, and these papers are partly a record of
that experiment.
